explanations.explanation: Habakkuk says it plainly: "…I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds." (Habakkuk 3:2) He heard the report, and he stands in awe of what the LORD has done. I think he's standing there with his mouth open.

Doubt is a fair guess. But in this prayer he says, "…I have heard the report of You; I stand in awe, O LORD, of Your deeds." (Habakkuk 3:2) That's a man who heard the report and stands in awe. Awe is what the verse gives us.

Nothing in the verse says Habakkuk wants to unhear anything. He says he has heard the report of the LORD and he stands in awe of His deeds (Habakkuk 3:2). Awe is the kind of feeling that makes you lean in, not cover your ears. I think he's leaning in, friend.

explanations.answer: Revive them and make them known
explanations.explanation: Habakkuk asks, "Revive them in these years; make them known in these years." (Habakkuk 3:2) He's heard what the LORD has done, and he wants those deeds alive in his own time. Notice he says "these years" twice. I think he means it, like a man tapping the table.

explanations.answer: Keep them safe in the past
explanations.explanation: Plenty of good things get tucked safely in the past. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I can tell you nothing gets better back there. Habakkuk asks for the opposite: "Revive them in these years; make them known in these years." (Habakkuk 3:2) He wants those deeds out where people can see them now.

Asking for an explanation would be a different prayer. Habakkuk asks the LORD to "Revive them in these years; make them known in these years." (Habakkuk 3:2) The verse never asks for a full explanation first. Awe doesn't need a footnote.

"In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (Habakkuk 3:2) That's a short prayer with a big ask. Habakkuk sets wrath and mercy side by side and asks for mercy to be remembered. I think a prayer this honest is hard to pray, and he prays it anyway.

Vengeance sounds like it could fit a prayer with this much thunder coming. But Habakkuk asks, "In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (Habakkuk 3:2) Wrath is in the verse, and so is his request for mercy right next to it. He's praying for mercy, not for payback.

Justice is a good word, and this prayer is full of the LORD going forth. But the word Habakkuk picks is mercy: "In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (Habakkuk 3:2) Wrath is named, and mercy is what he asks the LORD to remember in the middle of it. One little word, and it's a different prayer.

Habakkuk says, "…His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth." (Habakkuk 3:3) The heavens are covered and the earth is filled. There's not a corner left over. That's a whole lot of glory, friend.

Take another look at the verse. Habakkuk says, "…His glory covered the heavens, and His praise filled the earth." (Habakkuk 3:3) So the statement is true. The glory covers the heavens while God comes from Teman, and the praise fills the earth too.

Habakkuk says, "rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden." (Habakkuk 3:4) The rays flash from His hand, and that's where the power is hidden. If that's what the hand looks like, I'd say take a seat and listen. I think this is a prophet who knows he's looking at something big.

The verse actually says it. Habakkuk says, "rays flashed from His hand, where His power is hidden." (Habakkuk 3:4) So the hand is where the power is hidden. The statement is true, and the rays are the part he can see.

Habakkuk says, "Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps." (Habakkuk 3:5) One out in front and one right behind. That's a picture of a very serious arrival. It's a heavy line, so I'll let the text speak for itself.

Angels and singers would make this a parade. But Habakkuk says, "Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps." (Habakkuk 3:5) That's what goes before Him and what follows. This verse is no parade, friend.

Wind and fire fit the storm feel of this whole prayer, so I see the guess. But Habakkuk names something else: "Plague went before Him, and fever followed in His steps." (Habakkuk 3:5) Plague goes first and fever follows. Those are the two the text gives us.

It goes the other way. Habakkuk says, "the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed." (Habakkuk 3:6) That's the earth after God stands and measures it. Mountains are supposed to be the sturdy ones, and these crumble.

Right, and the verse is plain about it. God stands, measures the earth and startles the nations, and "the ancient mountains crumbled; the perpetual hills collapsed." (Habakkuk 3:6) Mountains are the thing we call solid. Meanwhile I can't even get my dough to hold its shape.

Habakkuk says, "His ways are everlasting." (Habakkuk 3:6) Look at what comes right before it: ancient mountains crumbling and perpetual hills collapsing. Those are the things we call permanent, and they go down. His ways don't.

Changing is a fair guess, since everything around is crumbling in this verse. But Habakkuk says, "His ways are everlasting." (Habakkuk 3:6) The mountains and hills go, and His ways stay. That's the whole contrast.

Slow doesn't show up anywhere in the verse. Habakkuk says, "His ways are everlasting." (Habakkuk 3:6) He's describing how long His ways last, not how fast they go. The mountains crumble and the hills collapse, and His ways keep standing.
Habakkuk says, "I saw the tents of Cushan in distress…" (Habakkuk 3:7) Cushan is the first of two names in that verse. Distress is the picture he gives.
Peace is a nice picture, but it isn't what Habakkuk saw. He says, "I saw the tents of Cushan in distress…" (Habakkuk 3:7) Distress is the word. These tents were not settled and quiet.
A party in the tents would be a different verse. Habakkuk says, "I saw the tents of Cushan in distress…" (Habakkuk 3:7) He's describing distress, not a celebration.

Habakkuk says, "The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high." (Habakkuk 3:10) He pictures the deep like a person, loud and with its hands up. When the mountains quake and the water sweeps by, even the deep joins in. That's some crowd.

Sleeping would be the quiet option, but that's not what Habakkuk pictures. He says, "The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high." (Habakkuk 3:10) Roaring and lifting hands is a different picture from sleeping and hiding its face.

Bowing and going silent sounds respectful, and I see why you'd go there. But Habakkuk says, "The deep roared with its voice and lifted its hands on high." (Habakkuk 3:10) It roars, so it isn't silent. The verse says it lifts its hands on high, and it never mentions bowing.

Habakkuk says, "You marched across the earth with fury; You threshed the nations in wrath." (Habakkuk 3:12) This is a heavy part of the prayer, and I won't dress it up. Habakkuk says it straight, and so does the text.

The verse says it right out. Habakkuk says, "You marched across the earth with fury; You threshed the nations in wrath." (Habakkuk 3:12) So the statement is true. It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't soften it.

Habakkuk says, "You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed." (Habakkuk 3:13) The verse before has the fury and the wrath. This verse names what He went forth for: salvation. Both are in the same prayer, and the text lets them stand together.

Testing is a natural guess for a prayer about hard times. But Habakkuk says, "You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed." (Habakkuk 3:13) The word is save. The verse gives no word about testing.

I see why you'd pick it, since wrath and nations are in the verse before. Habakkuk does say the LORD threshed the nations in wrath (Habakkuk 3:12). But the word in this verse is salvation: "You went forth for the salvation of Your people, to save Your anointed." (Habakkuk 3:13)

Habakkuk says, "With his own spear You pierced his head…" (Habakkuk 3:14) It was his own spear, and the verse says it plainly. This is a heavy line, so I'll leave it at what the text says. The same verse says his warriors stormed out to scatter us.

explanations.answer: A smooth stone from a sling
explanations.explanation: That one is from another story. David, Jesse's son, struck Goliath, the Philistine champion, with a stone from his sling (1 Samuel 17:4, 12, 49). Here Habakkuk says something different: "With his own spear You pierced his head…" (Habakkuk 3:14) The weapon is the wicked one's own spear.

explanations.answer: A tent peg and a hammer
explanations.explanation: Tent pegs and hammers show up in another story. Jael, the wife of Heber, used a tent peg and a hammer (Judges 4:17, 21). But Habakkuk's verse says something else: "With his own spear You pierced his head…" (Habakkuk 3:14) The weapon is the wicked one's own spear.

Look at the last word. Habakkuk says the warriors stormed out "…gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak." (Habakkuk 3:14) The word is weak, not strong, so the statement doesn't match the text. The picture is of warriors gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak.

Habakkuk says the warriors came out "…gloating as though ready to secretly devour the weak." (Habakkuk 3:14) So the statement is false, because the word is weak and not strong. The whole thing is a heavy picture, and one word changes it.

Habakkuk says, "You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters." (Habakkuk 3:15) The waters churn. We're back at the sea from earlier in the prayer, and it's still stirred up. That's a whole lot of water getting tossed around.

Drying up would be a quiet ending to a loud scene. But Habakkuk says, "You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters." (Habakkuk 3:15) The waters are stirred up, not gone. The sea is still there and still moving.

Water turning to blood is another story. In Egypt the water of the Nile was turned to blood (Exodus 7:20). Habakkuk's verse says something else: "You trampled the sea with Your horses, churning the great waters." (Habakkuk 3:15) The waters churn.

Habakkuk says, "I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound." (Habakkuk 3:16) He trembles within, and his lips quiver at the sound. A prayer that big goes right through a man. I think anyone would shake after hearing all that.
Relaxing is the opposite of what the verse says. Habakkuk says, "I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound." (Habakkuk 3:16) He doesn't settle back in his chair. He shakes.

I love a good laugh, but this verse doesn't have one. Habakkuk says, "I heard and trembled within; my lips quivered at the sound." (Habakkuk 3:16) His lips quiver at the sound. That's trembling, not laughing.

Habakkuk says, "Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us." (Habakkuk 3:16) He's shaking inside, and he still says he must wait patiently. That's a hard kind of waiting. I think waiting and shaking at the same time is its own skill.

Habakkuk is a prophet himself, so I see why the word came to mind. But the verse says, "Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us." (Habakkuk 3:16) The day of distress is for the people who invade. Prophets aren't named here.

Shepherds come to mind, since sheep come up in the next verse. But Habakkuk says, "Yet I must wait patiently for the day of distress to come upon the people who invade us." (Habakkuk 3:16) The people it comes upon are the ones who invade. Shepherds aren't in this verse.

The list doesn't stop at the crops, so I'd take another look. Habakkuk goes on to say, "…the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls…" (Habakkuk 3:17) So the animals are in the list too. The statement is false, because the sheep and cattle are part of it.

Habakkuk's list goes past the crops. He says, "…the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls…" (Habakkuk 3:17) So the sheep and cattle are in the list too, right along with the crops. That makes the statement false.

Habakkuk says, "…yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (Habakkuk 3:18) The list before it is full of things that aren't happening, and he still says yet. That one little word carries the whole verse. This is the happiest part of the prayer.

Walking away would be a very human move when the fields produce no food. But Habakkuk says, "…yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (Habakkuk 3:18) He doesn't walk away. He rejoices.

Bargaining isn't anywhere in this prayer. Habakkuk says, "…yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (Habakkuk 3:18) There's no deal on the table. He just rejoices, even when the fields produce no food.

Habakkuk says, "GOD the Lord is my strength…" (Habakkuk 3:19) He says it after that whole list of crops and animals. The Lord is his strength, plain and simple. I think that's a sturdy place to stand.
The verse says it plainly. Habakkuk says, "GOD the Lord is my strength…" (Habakkuk 3:19) So the statement is true, even with the fields producing no food. The verse names the Lord as his strength.

Habakkuk says, "He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights!" (Habakkuk 3:19) A deer and the heights go together nicely. I think it's a picture of a man with steady feet in high places. Not bad for someone who was trembling a few verses ago.

A lion is strong, so I see the guess. But Habakkuk says, "He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights!" (Habakkuk 3:19) The animal is a deer. The verse is about his feet on the heights.

An ox is a great worker, and I respect that. But Habakkuk says, "He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights!" (Habakkuk 3:19) The animal in the verse is a deer. It's his feet that the LORD makes like a deer's.
